about: The procedures of the work around a feature: tests, errors, bugs, refactors, security, documentation, the database, deploy, working under a lead, and keeping this knowledge base current.

rows.title: Playbook: write the tests (first)
rows.summary: One file `tests Name` in `test/`, one `@test` per acceptance criterion: the normal case, the edge cases and each error. Use only the names the task gives; create the rows a test reads before reading them; await once and keep the result.
body: 1. From the acceptance criteria, list what to check: the normal case, the empty or missing case, each error (`404`, `409`, `422`).
2. Write `test/<component>_test.nuc`:
```nuclear
// The tests of authors.
tests Authors
@test("adds an author and finds it by name")
addsAndFinds() void
authors = inject<AuthorsAppComponent>()
made = ~authors.add(NewAuthor(name = "Ursula"))
expect(made.isOk)
found = ~authors.byName("Ursula")
expect(found.value.name == "Ursula")
@test("a missing author is not found")
missing() void
authors = inject<AuthorsAppComponent>()
found = ~authors.byName("nobody")
expect(found.error.status == 404)
3. Rules:
- a test method returns `void`; `inject<X>()` gives an instance; `~` awaits; `expect(condition)` checks;
- a `Result` is kept and read: `isOk`, `value`, `error` (`error.status`);
- backend databases start **empty** in every test: first create the rows (through the code that adds them, or `~repository.save(Entity(...))`);
- never `inject<X>()` a class the task does not name; when only models are declared, build them and check their fields;
- mobile and web: `@mock([Repository])` on the group and `when(...).thenReturn(Ok(x))`;
- an agent's model in a test: `FakeModel(["answer"])`.
4. `nuclear check .` (the tests compile with the code); `nuclear test`.
5. A test that fails because the code is wrong is reported, never deleted or weakened.

rows.title: Playbook: fix the compiler's errors
rows.summary: `nuclear check --json`, then `nuclear fix` applies every exact fix; for what is left, read each error's message and its card (`error:<code>`), fix exactly what it says at its line, and check again. The first error of a file often causes the others.
body:
1. `nuclear check --json` (a piece: `--platform

`). Each error has `code`, `line`, `col`, `message` and often `fix`.
2. `nuclear fix <file|folder>`: applies the exact fixes (a habit of another language, a library name, a missing `~`).
3. For each error left, top to bottom:
- read its message: it usually names the right word;
- fetch its card: `nuclear-graph card error:<code>` (the cause, an example, the fix, the errors it comes with);
- change only that line or declaration.
4. Check again. Repeat until `[]`.
What helps:
- `N0022` (a habit of another language) hides the other errors of its line: fix it first.
- `N0106` (an undefined name) after `N0105`: the name was created inside a block and read outside it.
- `N0114` names the Nuclear member to use; `N0220` and `N0219` name the closest real class or argument.
- `N0301` and `N0302` are not typos: the call is not allowed by the architecture; move it to the right kind.
- An error in a file of `build/`: never fix it there; it comes from a `.nuc`.
- The same error after three tries is not a typo: the approach is wrong; read the kind's card again or escalate.

rows.title: Playbook: fix a failing test
rows.summary: Run `nuclear test`, give its output to `nuclear explain` to get the message and the `.nuc` lines, decide whether the code or the test is wrong, fix that one file and run again. Three rounds at most; then report.
body: 1. `nuclear test` → the output. `nuclear explain` (the output on stdin) answers the message, a hint and the `.nuc` lines, never the generated code's.
2. Decide which side is wrong:
- the test reads a row nobody created → the test (`pitfall:test-reads-an-empty-database`);
- the test expects what the spec does not say → the test;
- the code answers something else than the criterion → the code.
3. Fix that one file: the piece the lines name.
4. `nuclear check .`, `nuclear test` again.
5. After three rounds on the same test, stop: report the test, what was tried and why it still fails.

how do I read a test failure
how do I debug a failing test

rows.title: Playbook: fix a bug
rows.summary: Reproduce it with the smallest failing test, find the root cause in the `.nuc` (never in `build/`), fix it once in the shared code after finding every caller, and leave the new test in place.
body: 1. Reproduce: a `@test` that shows the bug, and run it.
2. Find the cause in the `.nuc`. Many bugs are a habit of another language; search the errors shelf with the behaviour or the message.
3. Find every caller of what you change (the project map `.nuclear/map.md`; `nuclear check .` after each step says what broke).
4. Fix it once, at the root.
5. The new test and every old one pass; `nuclear check .` reports nothing.
6. Say in two lines: the cause and the fix.

how does the agent diagnose a bug

rows.title: Playbook: refactor without changing behaviour
rows.summary: Run the tests first; move or rename in small steps, each one checked by the compiler; keep the platform's architecture; do mechanical rewrites one file at a time; no test is deleted.
body: 1. `nuclear test`: what passes now must pass at the end.
2. Find every caller of what moves (the project map; `nuclear check .` after each step).
3. Small steps, each green.
4. Keep the architecture: a use case is used only from its `appcomponent`; other components see only the `appcomponent`.
5. Mechanical rewrites (a field renamed in N files): one order per file.
6. Report what moved, what was deleted and why.
A refactor that needs to understand several files at once is led by a frontier model; its mechanical steps go one file at a time.

rows.title: Playbook: review a change for security
rows.summary: Check, from the most to the least severe: input validated at every boundary, access control on what belongs to a user, no secret in the code, queries only through the repository, user paths never joined unchecked, errors that leak nothing, known dependencies. Each finding has its line, an attack and the fix in Nuclear.
body: - **Input**: every model that comes from outside has its rule decorators (`@minLength`, `@maxLength`, `@min`, `@max`, `@pattern`, `@email`, `@url`, `@required`).
- **Access**: on mobile and web, `@acl` and guards on what belongs to a user. The backend has no guards yet: a use case that needs them checks the caller itself, and that is said in the review.
- **Secrets**: none in the code; `env("VAR")`.
- **Data**: queries only through the repository's builder; never text joined into a query.
- **Files and URLs** from a user: never joined or fetched without checking.
- **Errors**: a `Result` error with a message for the user, never internals.
- **Dependencies** in `config.nuc`: known and pinned.
For each finding: `severity | line | problem | fix`. No finding is "maybe": show the input that breaks it or leave it out. The reviewer reports; it does not change the code.

rows.title: Playbook: document what was built
rows.summary: Say what it is for, then how to use it, then how it works inside; show Nuclear, never generated code; name files and commands exactly; give every declaration a one-line `//` comment, because the project map and the agents read it.
body: - A `//` line above a declaration is its description: `nuclear check` copies it to `.nuclear/map.md`, which agents read instead of every file.
- A run's journal: what was built (each file and what it declares), how it was checked (the compiler, the tests, the review, with results), what is left.
- A document for people: who reads it and what they need first; short sentences; every Nuclear example must pass `nuclear check`.
- Plans and pending work are not documentation.

what does the documenter write

rows.title: Playbook: change the database's schema (backend)
rows.summary: Change the entity, then `nuclear migrate make "<message>"` writes one migration (the entities minus the last migration), `nuclear migrate` applies it, `nuclear migrate down` reverts the last one and `nuclear migrate status` lists them; the same in every backend dialect.
body: 1. Change the entity's `.nuc` (a new field, a length, a relation).
2. `nuclear build`.
3. `nuclear migrate make "add the year of a book"`: one migration file.
4. `nuclear migrate` (or `migrate up`); `nuclear migrate down` to revert the last one; `--to <migration>` on either reaches that one.
5. `nuclear migrate status` lists every migration as applied or pending.
6. From an agent, the MCP tool `project_migrate(project, action)` does each of these (`status`, `make` with `message`, `up`, `down`, `to`): `make`, `up` and `down` ask the user first.

A new column that is not optional needs a default: the rows that exist need a value (`make` warns of it, and of every drop). The pending migrations run in one transaction (`--transaction all`, the default; `each`: one per migration; `none`): PostgreSQL and SQLite keep nothing of a run that fails; MySQL and MariaDB cannot undo a schema change, and the message says so. A rename is written by `make` as a drop and an add: edit the file into a rename to keep the data. A database that already has the tables (made by `createTables = true`, or by hand): `nuclear migrate --fake` marks the migrations applied without running them. The history is the table `migrations`, one row per migration applied, in the order of their names; a change of a table's key is refused at `make`.

rows.title: Playbook: the pipeline's commands, locally and on a server
rows.summary: `.nuclear/builder.json` holds the commands of each stage; add `seed`, `integration` and `deploy` for the deploy stage. `nuclear-builder ci` runs them where you are, and `nuclear-builder export github|gitlab|bitbucket` writes the CI file that runs the same ones on every push.
body: ```json
"commands": {
"seed": ["nuclear migrate"],
"integration": ["nuclear test -- -m integration"],
"deploy": ["docker compose up -d --build"]
"branches": ["main", "feature/**"]
- The defaults (check, build, install, test) come from the platform's CLI.
- `nuclear-builder ci [check|test|security|artifacts|deploy]` runs the server's stages locally: see what the server will see before pushing.
- The agent stages run on your machine; the server checks their result.
- The shell of the Builder runs nothing that is not in `.nuclear/builder.json`.
- There is no generated Dockerfile yet: the deploy command is yours.

rows.title: Playbook: when a task is beyond the agent at work
rows.summary: Say it early and plainly: what was asked, what is missing or too large, and the options: split the task, give the missing facts, or give it to a stronger model (another team member in the Builder, or a frontier agent over MCP). Never invent to keep going, and never report as done what was not checked.
body: **When.**
- The spec names nothing to build, or a fact is missing and cannot be found.
- The task needs a design decision, or to understand several files at once.
- The spec, a file or the dependencies of a piece do not fit in the context window.
- A capabilities row says the platform cannot do it yet.
- The same step failed three times.

**How it is found.** The plan of a spec says it before any code: the capabilities rows whose trigger words the spec writes ("authentication" on the backend, "form" on the web), a spec longer than the model reads at once, a plan without pieces or with too many.
**What to say** (to the user in the chat, or in the run's journal):
1. what was asked, in one line;
2. what is beyond the agent, and why (the limit's name: one file per order, the context window, a decision, a missing fact, a platform limit);
3. what was done so far, and that it was checked (or not);
4. the options:
- **split it**: the pieces the agent can do now;
- **give the facts**: the exact question (which fields? which rule when X?);
- **a stronger model**: the station given to a team member worked by a frontier agent or API model (`nuclear-builder team member update`), or the user's agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) over MCP;
- **not possible yet**: the platform's limit and what exists instead.
**Never**: guess a name, a field or a rule; write the easy half and call it done; delete or weaken a test.

rows.title: Playbook: a frontier model leads and writes over MCP
rows.summary: The lead (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku or another model over MCP) understands the spec and the project, generates the standard code, writes the rest in small pieces, validates with the compiler and the tests and corrects only what failed. The local developer it once gave small orders to is on standby (ADR-platform-0013): no `developer_*` tool is registered.
body: 0. Nothing about Nuclear known yet: `nuclear_start` first (the rules, the work cycle, the atlas; `nuclear_doc` for a topic); then `graph_strategy` with the user's own words.

1. `project_inspect`; for every resource the spec names, `generate_resource` (fields from the spec, `api_inspect`, or the documentation with `web_search` and `web_read`; ask the user when none gives them).

2. Write only what the generators did not, one piece at a time: the path, the kind, every name and signature, the pieces it uses, the acceptance criterion it serves. Before writing `.nuc`: `nuclear_brief(<platform>)` and `graph_search`. A use case is wired with `generate_usecase` (its alias in the facade; backend: its route).
3. Validate: `nuclear_check(path = <project>)` says `ok`; the project's tests pass (`nuclear test`).
4. Correct only what failed or is wrong; never rewrite what passed.

**A whole spec in the Builder.** A team's stations are worked by its members (agents or API models), each assigned by the tech lead (`concept:loop`); `nuclear-builder retry <run>` runs a failed one again, the steps that passed kept.

rows.title: Playbook: connect Claude Code, Codex or Cursor to NuclearLang
rows.summary: Set up the AI services, then add `nuclear-mcp` to the client as an MCP server named `nuclear`. The client then has the generators, the graph and the compiler as tools.
body: ```sh
nuclear-builder setup                                # once: the services, and MCP clients' access to the graph
claude mcp add --scope user nuclear -- nuclear-mcp   # Claude Code
codex mcp add nuclear -- nuclear-mcp                 # Codex
- Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`): `{ "mcpServers": { "nuclear": { "command": "nuclear-mcp" } } }`.
- OpenCode (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`): `{ "mcp": { "nuclear": { "type": "local", "command": ["nuclear-mcp"], "enabled": true } } }`.
- VS Code: *Settings and integrations* (`Ctrl+Alt+S`) has a button per client.
- Check it: ask the client to call `graph_search` with "what is nuclear".
- The graph refuses the client: `nuclear-graph connect mcp --scopes read,write`, with the graph running.
- The server registers no `developer_*` tool: the local models are on standby (ADR-platform-0013, `limit:remote-agents-only`).

rows.title: Playbook: set up the AI services (the Smart Graph, the MCP server, Nuclear Chat)
rows.summary: Run `nuclear-builder setup --profile remote --yes` in a terminal, *Nuclear: Set Up the AI Services* in VS Code, or the last step of the installer (no question). It installs the Smart Graph, its model and the MCP server, adds the server to every AI client, loads the knowledge base and starts the Smart Graph and Nuclear Chat, now and at every login. `remote` is the one profile: the local models are on standby.
body: ```sh
nuclear-builder setup --profile remote --yes   # no questions
nuclear-builder setup --status                 # what is installed and running
nuclear-builder setup --clients                # the MCP server in a client installed later
nuclear-builder setup --remove                 # takes the services away (the graph's data stays; --all: everything it made)
1. **What it needs**: NuclearLang with its AI archive (the set-up and the services bring their own Python, the Smart Graph its own model); from the source tree also `uv`.

2. **What was local**: on a machine an earlier version set up with a local profile, a first step takes away the Nuclear Developer's service and launcher, the models NuclearLang downloaded and Ollama when NuclearLang installed it, writes `ai.env` as `remote` and says the GB freed.

3. **Install**: the Smart Graph, its model and the MCP server, the MCP server added to every AI client found (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build), the knowledge base into the graph (seconds with the vectors the release computed; without them, about ten minutes on a processor), the Smart Graph and Nuclear Chat started. A step that fails says why; try again from it.
- Afterwards, give your agent the MCP server: `claude mcp add --scope user nuclear -- nuclear-mcp`, or the buttons of *Settings and integrations* in VS Code.
- `--profile lite|medium|hard` is refused: the local models are on standby (`faq:local-models`).
- In CI or a script: the installer's `--no-ai` skips it.
- From the source tree: `installer/install.sh --ai` (it needs `uv`), or `--ai-runtime` to build the AI archive as a release brings it.
- The editors run the same set-up as a process: `nuclear-builder setup --plan --json` and `--events`.

rows.title: Playbook: keep the knowledge base current after every change
rows.summary: After a feature of the ecosystem: `nuclear-graph knowledge build`, fix what it reports, review the hand-written rows whose sources changed, `nuclear-graph knowledge check` until clean, then `nuclear-graph ingest`. A new tool, error, kind or limit gets its row in the same change.
body: 1. **What changed?** A command, an MCP tool, a route, a kind, a decorator, a diagnostic, a version, an example, a document: their rows are generated. A new idea, capability, limit, failure or procedure: write its row by hand.
2. `nuclear-graph knowledge build`. It rewrites the generated assets and validates everything: a link to a missing row, a duplicated id or target code in an agents' row stops it.

3. **Curated rows.** For each line `review: <id> was written from <source>, which changed`: read the change; update the row in `assets/<shelf>/<file>.json` if it no longer holds, or confirm it with `nuclear-graph knowledge review <id>`.

4. **New knowledge by hand**: a row in the right shelf with its `id`, `type`, `title`, `summary`, `body`, `keys`, `asks`, `links` and `sources`. A new diagnostic's relations and example go in `assets/errors/diagnostics.overlay.json`.
5. `nuclear-graph knowledge check` must print that every row is what the tree gives now.
6. `nuclear-graph ingest`: the graph learns the new revision.
7. Ask it: `nuclear-graph search "<a question the change answers>"` must return the new row first. Add the question to the retrieval tests.
The session's end hook runs the check: a change of the ecosystem is not finished while it fails.

rows.title: Playbook: size a task, then do it or propose Nuclear Builder
rows.summary: Before any work, count the files and lines a request would change and whether it adds a feature. Small (<= 3 files, <= 100 lines) and medium (<= 10 files, <= 400 lines) without a new feature: the agent does it and says what it touched. Larger, a new feature or several specs: propose Nuclear Builder (one spec or several, one run) with the count as the reason; the user decides.
body: 1. Read what the request touches (`project_inspect`, the files) and count: the files changed or created, about how many lines, and whether it adds a feature: a new screen, endpoint, entity, component or use case, or a changed contract or schema.
2. Decide by the table:
| Size | Measure | Who does it |
| small | <= 3 files, <= 100 lines, no feature | the agent, now |
| medium | <= 10 files, <= 400 lines, no new feature | the agent, saying which files it touched |
| large | more, a new feature, or several specs | Nuclear Builder, proposed with the count; the user decides |
3. Say the size in one line before starting (`small: 2 files, ~40 lines, no feature`). When the work grows past its size, stop and say so.
4. A large task: name what each spec would hold and why it is large; with the user's yes, `spec_create` each spec and `run_start` one run.

The numbers follow code review practice, not a law: Google's engineering practices (about 100 lines a reasonable change, 1,000 usually too large), the SmartBear/Cisco review study (defects missed past about 400 lines), a study of npm pull requests (accepted ones mostly change 5 to 15 files).
asks: should I use nuclear builder for this
is this task small or large
